content.title: Artemis II makes successful splashdown after historic moon mission: 'Perfect bullseye'
content.text: After 10 days and a history-making mission to the Moon, the four astronauts aboard Artemis II returned to Earth Friday night, ending their journey with a splashdown off the coast of San Diego.Commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Canada’s Jeremy Hansen hit the atmosphere traveling Mach 33, or 33 times the speed of sound, a blistering blur not seen since NASA’s Apollo moonshots of the 1960s and 1970s. Their Orion capsule, dubbed Integrity, made the plunge on autopilot.The tension in Mission Control mounted as the capsule became engulfed in red-hot plasma during peak heating and entered a planned communication blackout.All eyes were on the capsule's life-protecting heat shield that had to withstand thousands of degrees during reentry. On the spacecraft’s only other test flight, in 2022, with no one on board, the shield’s charred exterior came back looking as pockmarked as the moon.The recovery ship USS John P. Murtha awaited the crew’s arrival off the San Diego coast, along with a squadron of military planes and helicopters, while the astronauts' families watched from Mission Control's viewing room. Cheers erupted when the capsule emerged from blackout and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean. "A perfect bull’s-eye splashdown," reported Mission Control's Rob Navias.After splashdown, the astronauts were evaluated inside the capsule before being removed and flown via helicopter to the USS John P. Murtha. Before leaving the splashdown site, the astronauts were seen getting their first breath of fresh air on their home planet. Once arriving on the ship, the crew will spend most of the night in the medical bay being monitored. President Donald Trump congratulated NASA on the successful mission, writing on Truth Social, "Congratulations to the Great and Very Talented Crew of Artemis II. The entire trip was spectacular, the landing was perfect and, as President of the United States, I could not be more proud! I look forward to seeing you all at the White House soon. We’ll be doing it again and then, next step, Mars!"NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman celebrated the Artemis II crew as "ambassadors from humanity to the stars" after the astronauts splashed down.Isaacman said America is "back in the business of sending astronauts to the moon" with regular missions ahead and a 2028 moon landing and future lunar base.However, reentry into Earth’s atmosphere didn't come without risks.The Orion capsule’s life-protecting heat shield must withstand temperatures of thousands of degrees as it hurtles back at roughly 34,965 feet per second — about 23,840 mph. The crew did not plan to take manual control unless an emergency arose. The last time NASA and the Department of Defense coordinated a lunar crew’s reentry was during Apollo 17 in 1972.Artemis II lifted off from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on April 1, renewing global interest in space exploration and marking a major step toward establishing a sustainable human presence on the Moon.Unlike Apollo 11 in 1969, the mission did not land on or orbit the Moon. Instead, it broke Apollo 13’s distance record, making the crew the farthest humans have ever traveled from Earth. They reached 252,756 miles, surpassing the 1970 record of 248,655 miles.During the flyby, the astronauts spent more than six hours observing and documenting the far side of the Moon—previously seen only by robotic missions. They also witnessed a total solar eclipse, which Glover said “just blew all of us away.”Koch, the first woman to fly around the Moon, described the craters as looking like a “lampshade with tiny pinprick holes and the light shining through.”But being hundreds of thousands of miles away from Earth didn't come without its challenges that the astronauts gladly welcomed. One of the most high-profile predicaments involved the toilet trouble the crew faced for most of the trip, forcing them to use old-time bags and funnels. “We can’t explore deeper unless we are doing a few things that are inconvenient,” Koch said, “unless we’re making a few sacrifices, unless we’re taking a few risks, and those things are all worth it.”“You do a lot of testing on the ground, but your final test is when you get this hardware to space and it’s a doozy," Hansen added. Next year, Artemis III will see astronauts practice docking their capsule with a lunar landing or two in orbit around Earth. Artemis IV will attempt to land a crew of two near the moon’s south pole in 2028.The crew on Thursday also expressed love and appreciation for their families, who supported them throughout the mission. Wiseman spoke about his two daughters, Glover shared encouragement for his four daughters, Koch said it felt like her nine nieces and nephews were with her, and Hansen told his children he learns as much from them as they do from him.But even as the world watched in awe at the 10-day mission, Wiseman reminded humanity to "pause and remember that this is a beautiful planet and a very special place in our universe." "We should all cherish what we have been gifted,” he said.___________The Associated Press contributed to this report.
